On February 26 the hon. member for North Battleford (Mr. McIntosh) explained to the house at some length that he had received a communication from his constituency stating that some of the enumerators had not been paid for the work they did in preparing the voters' lists. I have made inquiries on the subject and have received the following letter signed by Watson Sellar, comptroller of the treasury:
Section 48 of the Franchise Act requires the auditor general to tax all accounts submitted by the enumerators. On February 14, and again on the 15th, this office received applications for cheques from the auditor general to pay the accounts for North Battleford. Cheques were drawn on each day, and delivered to the auditor general, for they are mailed from his offices.
I believe these payments cleaned up all accounts for that constituency, with one exception. In this case, it is believed a claim could be made, but the person concerned has not sent in an account.
This office has no arrears to catch up with respect to payments to enumerators. Cheques are drawn the same day as the application is made by the auditor general. To date, approximately 39,000 cheques have been issued, and by the time a further 1,000 will have been received, the work should be completed.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I call your attention to the fact that when the hon. member raised this question on February 26 all the cheques in payment of these accounts had gone out ten or twelve days before. I submit to the hon. gentleman that although he might not have got as much publicity as in that way, he could have obtained this information more easily, and without taking up the time of the house, if he had telephoned to either the auditor general or the comptroller of the treasury.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Hon. E. N. RHODES (Minister of Finance) moved the second reading of Bill No. 10, to amend the Farmer's Creditors Arrangement Act, 1934.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO FARMERS' CREDITORS ARRANGEMENT ACT, 1934
speechtext:
It is not my intention, Mr. Speaker, to delay the house for more than a few minutes on the second reading of this very important bill, but because I believe there is a misunderstanding in the minds of some members of this house as well as many members of the general public in regard to the question of farmers' debts, I do want to bring to their attention a few facts to demonstrate the need for the legislation known as the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act.
Figures which I secured from one of the chartered banks, accompanying a chart published in its recent monthly bulletin in regard to the farm cash income of Canada, show that for the years 1926, 1927, 1928 and 1929, the four pre-depression years the total farm cash income in Canada was $4,012,000,000. In the years 1931, 1932, 1933 and 1934, the last four years, the farm cash income was only $1,744,000,000, so in those four years there was a drop of $2,268,000,000, or 57 per cent. That is the cause of the present terrific burden of farm debts which really makes this legislation necessary. The average drop in cash revenue per farm in Canada for the four years amounts to $3,136; that is the loss in revenue to the average farmer during that period. That total amount of $2,268,000,000 would have been sufficient to pay every farm debt in Canada, to wipe the slate clean and leave over an amount equal to $i,000 per farmer. That drop in revenue of $3,136 per farm resulted from a drop in the price level of farm products. It has not been due, as some people seem to think, to crop failures through drought or otherwise. It is true there have been crop failures in some areas, but on the whole production during the last four years has equalled the production of predepression years. I think the fact should be emphasized, that the decreased revenue is due to a drop in price levels.
The article to which I have referred indicates that the farm cash income, converted into dollars having the same purchasing power as in 1926-and I quote these figures to show that the drop in farm purchasing power, while not quite as great as the drop in money income, has been very severe indeed-for the four years from 1926 to 1929, would be $3,994,000,000, while the farm cash income,

Farmers' Creditors Act-Mr. Coote
computed on the same basis, for the four years 1931 to 1934, would amount to $2,384,000,000. As a result there has been a loss of purchasing power to the farmers in the last four years amounting to $1,610,000,000. When you consider that the net cash income of the farmers in Canada is the greatest source of purchasing power in the country it is no wonder that a business man in western Canada should have said a year ago, "If it is true, as some modernists say, that there is no hell, where has business gone, anyway?"
On Monday last I gave the house figures showing the loss of farm purchasing power in Canada for the past four years as compared with Australia, and I need not go into the matter again. I estimated that the drop in farm revenue in Canada was $852,000,000 more than it would have been if we had had the same money policy as Australia. There is an impression in this country, and I think the statement has been made in this house, that farmers in Canada are better off than are the farmers in most other countries in the world. I want to say, Mr. Speaker, that this impression is absolutely wrong. The hon. member for Willow Bunch (Mr. Donnelly) gave us very good proof just a couple of days ago that the farmers of the United States are not as badly off as we are in Canada and I should like to direct the attention of the house to the situation of the farmers in the Argentine, who have a sixty per cent exchange advantage over us. In the old days the Argentine peso, under the old parity, was worth forty-two cents in Canada. It is now worth twenty-five cents. If a shipment of corned beef or any other commodity from the Argentine to Canada brought the Argentine exporter $1,000 in Canadian currency, under the old parity, when the peso was worth forty-two cents, he would have converted his $1,000 into 2,380 pesos. At the present rate of exchange, however, he would receive 4,000 pesos, which gives him an advantage of sixty per cent as compared with the position he occupied previously.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO FARMERS' CREDITORS ARRANGEMENT ACT, 1934
speechtext: Is the hon. gentleman arguing in favour of the dumping regulations?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO FARMERS' CREDITORS ARRANGEMENT ACT, 1934
speechtext:
Farmers' Creditors Act-Mr. Coote
rate for any farmer to carry, and particularly for a man who has had his affairs rearranged under the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act. It is clear to all of us that if the board of review would write down his debts he must be in difficulties. In many cases however in connection with which action has been taken the farmer has been left with a rate of seven per cent on his remaining liabilities. In a great many cases-and I believe this might almost be said to be the rule adopted by one of the boards-they reduce the arrears of interest by one-third. The farmer with two-thirds of his arrears added to his principal and paying a rate of seven per cent is in most cases in a far worse position than if he had no arrears and was still paying eight per cent. I believe it is safe to say that only in extreme cases have boards of review set a rate lower than seven per cent,- and I am talking now about my own province, because I do not know how the boards function in the other provinces.
My reason for speaking of this is that loan companies seem to be exercised over the action of the board,-or pretend to be. I am informed that some of their eastern officials have travelled out to our province to interview the board and the provincial government, and to tell them that if this policy is adhered to there will be fatal reactions or repercussions. So far as I am concerned I wish to emphasize that seven per cent is too high a rate of interest for farmers to pay. I believe the act should be amended so as to fix a maximum rate of four per cent or five per cent. If that reduction will endanger the position of any of the loan companies then the legislation should be made wide enough so that the reduction may be carried right through to the persons who originally invested in the debentures or bonds of the mortgage company.
Finally I should like to bring to the attention of the house the actual position of the farmers who have been paying this rate of eight per cent for the last twenty or twenty-five years. I have before me a letter which was clipped from a western paper, and was sent to me. It arrived in my mail this morning. This is part of a letter written by a farmer in Saskatchewan to his creditor in Waterloo, Ontario, stating:
Received your notice calling for payment of $6,238.92. Some figures. This amount has grown from $4,000 in 1928, our last crop, to $6,238.92 this year. This is certainly some Tacket. I wish I could make money as fast. Your offer of giving $2 for every dollar paid on interest arrears is a step in the right direction but of no avail, as we have had no crop

this year to pay anything, so you can put a few more figures on for next year, they look nice anyway.
You will soon have it up to $10,090 on paper, and on paper it will remain unless you make a real adjustment of balance and give me a definite amount to pay.
I will now list a few figures. As you know, the original loan when assumed by me was $6,000.
He proceeded to show by figures what payments had been made, the amount totalling $8,355.96, and then he says:
I have paid $8,355.96, and according to notice, I still owe you more than I originally did.
That is the case with so many farmers. Here is a farmer in my own constituency, living only a few miles from my own farm, who has paid eight per cent on a loan of $500 for twenty years. That is, he has paid $800 interest, but he still owes the $500, and the mortgage company is still collecting eight per cent. Now if this man had had a loan at 5J per cent, which I think would have been a fair rate of interest, I think his loan would now be paid off and his farm be free of debt, but as it is he is still carrying that load of $500. When he applied to the farm loan board this year he was told that they were afraid they could not give him a loan large enough to meet all his liabilities. He wanted a loan of $2,000 on 240 acres. The matter is still under consideration by the board. I am not referring to the board's action at the moment. I just want to use this case for the sake of illustration. If there had been a reduction in the rate of interest of even one per cent, if this man had had to pay seven per cent instead of the eight per cent, and that one per cent had been used towards amortizing his loan, I think by this time he would have had it cut in two. I do want to see the rate of interest low enough so that these farmers can look forward with some reasonable expectation of having their farms cleared before they pass out from this world.
In conclusion, I want to urge upon the minister that before this bill is finally taken out of committee he should make the necessary amendment to the last section of the bill to provide a maximum rate of interest on farm mortgages for at least a term of years. I think that maximum should not be more than five per cent at the outside, and I would hope that it could be done at four per cent, and if necessary make it so that it will carry through to the original investor in the mortgage company's bonds. I do not want to bring the mortgage companies into the bankrupt class; there are so many farmers there now, and it would not give me any pleasure

Farmers' Creditors Act-Mr. Bothwell
to see any more people or corporations put into that position, but I think that is the best thing to do under the circumstances. I believe it is far better for these people to have a mortgage under which they will receive their money at five per cent than one at eight per cent when they are not going to get their money, and it is better for an investor to have a bond at three or four per cent when he is going to be paid than one at five per cent which he is afraid is not going to be made good.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO FARMERS' CREDITORS ARRANGEMENT ACT, 1934
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the amendments which are before the house are aimed at remedying some of the inadequacies of the act. I think it is imperative that those inadequacies be remedied, and remedied at once, because if the traditional delays of the law are going to overtake the administration of this act it will fail, and fail miserably, in its purpose. It is failing in part now because the delay of sixty days granted to the farmer who makes a proposal under the act, having expired in many cases before they have been disposed of by the board of review,_ the seizing creditor has been able to go on with his action or his execution.
I furthermore note that in Quebec at least that the act is inadequate in that no reference is made to a very common type of transaction by which a property is acquired, and there does not appear to be in the amendments any proposal to meet this inadequacy.
I would draw to the minister's attention that an accumulation of appeals and the delay which must elapse before they can be disposed of endangers the working of the act * itself.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO FARMERS' CREDITORS ARRANGEMENT ACT, 1934
speechtext:
Complaint has been made that this act in its operation has the effect of penalizing the local creditor possibly for the benefit of the mortgage companies and the secured creditor.
The complaint is also made that in the case of a first mortgage on land no reductions are ordinarily made excepting a reduction in the arrears of interest, and possibly a very small cut in the rate of interest. When a farmer finds it necessary to make application to the official under this act, and that official finds that a farmer is in such circumstances that he needs the benefit of the act, then it does seem to me that an adjustment should be made whereby that debtor should not be required to pay more than the legal rate of interest from that time on until he is able to get on his feet, that legal rate of interest being five per cent at the moment. The reduction that was referred to by the hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Coote) from
eight per cent to seven per cent is of no special value to that farmer at all because he is in such circumstances that he needs a greater reduction than that.
Then I believe, too, that all of these officials who have charge of administering the act should be instructed that they are not to approve of a scheme that only has the effect of penalizing the local merchants and the local people in the community in which the debtor lives and allows the mortgage _ company to get away with what is practically an increase in its security. That is actually what is happening at the present time.
_ I had a reply the other day from the minister in connection with the operation of this act in Swift Current. That reply stated that some thirteen applications, I think it was, had been dealt with and in one a formal order was made. Compromises were secured to the extent of some $52,000. I do not know how it worked out in all cases but I do know this, that one case that will be included within that $52,000, and in which there was a very substantial reduction amounting to several thousands of dollars, would have come about whether we had an official receiver there or not. The creditor who had to suffer the adjustment-we will call it that-stated that had the debtor approached him in the first place he would have made an adjustment himself, and possibly an even better adjustment than was made, without the intervention of the official referee.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO FARMERS' CREDITORS ARRANGEMENT ACT, 1934
speechtext: Why didn't he do it then?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO FARMERS' CREDITORS ARRANGEMENT ACT, 1934
speechtext:
He never was approached by the debtor. The debtor, immediately he knew something of the operation of the act, went to the official referee and made his proposition and the papers were sent out calling him into the official referee's office.
But the point I specially want to make is this, that in the operation of this act, while it should be beneficial to many farmers, and there are many farmers particularly in the west who need any benefits this act can afford, there is another class of person in the west who is also entitled to some consideration and whom I think this act should be extended to include. As the matter now stands the farmer is able to get an adjustment, as I said, at the expense of the local merchant and local business man, the local professional man, and so on. But the merchants in these country places are not able to collect their debts, and they are getting no reduction from the wholesaler. They need the benefit of an act such as this just as much as the farmer does. They are giving

Farmers' Creditors Act-Mr. Loucks
the farmer a reduction on his debt, not being paid in a great many instances, although they expect to get it over a period of years. But so far as the merchant is concerned he is getting no reduction, and consequently the merchant, the business man of every description and professional men are gradually going broke. I trust that the minister will give attention to that class of case and consider the advisability of extending the operation of this act to include some of the other classes who are being penalized at the present time just as much as the farmer is.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO FARMERS' CREDITORS ARRANGEMENT ACT, 1934
speechtext:
I have
no criticism to make of the remarks we have heard from the hon. member for Swift Current (Mr. Bothwell). He has pretty well stated the case in this house to-day, and I can endorse what he has said. The unfortunate thing is that throughout the little towns in western Canada the merchant has given security to the wholesaler, either by way of note or in some collateral form, and when he is asked to write down the debts due to him it is not very encouraging for him to find that he cannot get any money. But the wholesaler holds the local merchant to his indebtedness, one hundred cents on the dollar. In my opinion, so far as the local debts in our province are concerned, they could be cut in half if some money were available to take care of the local merchants after they have written down debts. If this were done it would stimulate trade right across the country and give the farmers and others a fresh start.
I may have big ideas, something perhaps beyond the power of this government to put into effect, but I do say that the situation is very serious indeed. I am still convinced that agriculture is the basic industry of the country, and if it were possible either to consolidate the debts of the farmers, not only in western Canada but throughout the dominion, and to write them down fifty per cent, it would have a very beneficial effect indeed. From one receiver I have received a letter informing me that the debts in his locality could be written down from $700,000 to 8300,000 if only ready money were available, and there would be no heed to go to the court of review. This morning I received a letter from a farmer who sold his farm in my district. On this farm he put up a house at a cost of $5,000. On moving to British Columbia he sold the farm and the purchaser owes a balance of $9,000 for it, and the purchaser is now applying to the receiver for a fifty per cent writing down. I have a

copy of a letter from the man in British Columbia-the man who sold the farm in question-and he now offers to take $4,500 in settlement of his claim for $9,000. But he wants ready money.
You will say, but what about $90,000,000 we have already voted for that very purpose. Well, I realize that that is a real move in the right direction, but I cannot help feeling that it will be only a drop in the bucket over the dominion when it comes to satisfying the applications that will flood in to the farm loan board. I have not the figures before me, and I can only speak from memory, but I believe that in 1933 the hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Coote), either in the committee on agriculture or in the banking and commerce committee, stated that the debts of the farmers throughout Canada amounted to $1,500,000,000-I am not sure of the amount. If that could be reduced by half, I can think of nothing that would so stimulate business. It would help matters very greatly if the government could issue enough money to wipe out this debt. I would be willing to tackle it. You may say, "But you are not a financier." Well, I know that I am not a financier, but I ask this question: What can the farmers do under present circumstances? If this debt could be written down to fifty cents on the dollar you would really have twice the security that you have now, because the farmers, with things as they are at present, will never be able to meet their obligations. They certainly cannot do so in the west.
I am not a pessimist who thinks that there is no hope for the country, but at the same time it is rather discouraging to the farmer to feel that he cannot get out of debt. The hon. member for Macleod suggests the reduction of interests. I have another alternative. I believe that if it were possible to have a moratorium at this time and to cut out interest it would give the farmers a chance, so that interest would not accumulate for the next five or ten years. If you could do that there would be more hope for the farmer. But when he looks at his mortgage to-day, when he compares his present liabilities with his indebtedness five or eight years ago, he sees that it has about doubled, and he sees no hope ahead; interest will continue around seven per cent. This is not very encouraging to the farmer. We have to face these things whether we are on this side of the house or sitting opposite, and I hope we shall all be big enough to get together on this question, because if agriculture is not once more placed

Farmers' Creditors Act

Mr. Loucks
on a prosperous basis there is no hope for the rest of the country. I think we are all agreed on that.
My hon. friend from Willow Bunch (Mr. Donnelly) has painted a very black picture of conditions in western Canada. I do not believe he did it intentionally, but I think he was exploiting the situation yesterday. In January I happened to be in Montana visiting my daughter, and I certainly did not find things there as rosy as he painted them. There was a processing tax of thirty cents a bushel on wheat and there was also a processing tax, which the hon. gentleman did admit, of three cents a pound on hogs; and my daughter told me that there was a personal tax on household effects. The assessor goes right into her house and assesses her silverware and other things, and even her watch is assessed. My son-in-law told me he had to get a licence for his car, and he had to pay a tax on his car on the first of January. And what about the condition of the people there? They are living in shacks, not- such buildings as we have in this country. The housing situation is bad, and if you went there you would endorse what I say. But what is their answer when you point this out to them? They say that if they put up a house they are assessed for it. They are taxed on everything conceivable, from a woman's jewellery, silverware and household effects right down. Down there the farmers feel that in Canada, at any rate, the Prime Minister has tried! to do something.

speechtext: I do not wish to interrupt the hon. gentleman, but I would ask him to confine himself to the subject.

speechtext:
I will try to do so, Mr. Speaker. Hon. gentlemen opposite say that the tariff is the source of the trouble. But I compared conditions in Canada with conditions in Montana when I was there last January and I did not find so much difference in the price of machinery. But even supposing any difficulty in that connection could be got over, that would not save the situation to-day.
While I agree that this amendment to the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act will be a help so far as the farmers are concerned, I believe we must igo further. Even with good crops in western Canada-and I am speaking about the west particularly because I am more familiar with it-the farmers, with the prevailing prices cannot recover. There are other aspects of the question. I know farmers in my constituency bought land at $70 or $75 an acre and I know it is impossible for them ever to meet their obligations because there
is no such earning capacity in any farm in western Canada. With wheat at $2 a bushel, there might be hope of writing off their debts but we cannot expect such prices for some time to come.
When I suggested, as I did recently that a moratorium be introduced and an assurance given to farmers that for five years interest would be wiped out, I was told that to do so would be ridiculous. The question was asked: What about the poor fellow who depends on that interest for his livelihood? Well, according to the figures given by the hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Coote), these people have been pretty well paid and in many cases the debt has been doubled. If I were holding a mortgage on a farm for S10,000 at seven per cent interest, knowing conditions as I do, as the mortgage companies and as individual lenders do, I would be very happy if any government were to come to my -rescue and say: If you will consider giving the mortgagor a chance and will wipe out the interest, probably we can assure you that at some time in the future you will get the principal. I think most people or companies who hold mortgages on farms to-day would be very glad should some such assurance be given-. If that were done, it would be a great help to the farmers of western Canada.
I want to stress the point again that I cannot see how the farmer is to ask merchants and professional men to write off 50 per cent of his debt and yet we cannot come to their rescue and give them a dollar to help them back on their feet. I know I am on this side of the house and I am speaking plainly. These are matters that we must consid-er and I do not care from which side the suggestion comes. Surely we are big enough when we are sent here -by the people to represent them as a whole. The h-on. member for Swift Current (Mr. Bothwell) made that very plain. He has given the situation as he knows it in his particular constituency and the same is true of m-e. We are hoping for a scheme which will prevent similar conditions from again arising in western Canada. The hon. member for Compton (Mr. Gobeil) beside me suggests: What about gambling? The farmers in the west say that the whole thing to-day is a gamble, but if we can get some of the streams dammed up under the scheme put forward by the Department of Agriculture, we shall forget that it is a gamble and I believe such a scheme is a move in the .right direction.
So far as gambling is concerned we have all had a lesson, but I will not speak further about that because I shall be called to order by the chair and rightly so. The Minister of

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act, introduced in this house last year by the hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. Rhodes) with the approval of the right hon. the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett), is now back before us for amendment.
This act may suit some of the provinces, but it is not in the interest of the province of Quebec, for it is doing more harm to .the credit of the farming class of Quebec than any other bill ever introduced in this house, except the conscription bill of 1917. When the prime minister moved the adoption of this bill, last year, he thought he had found the remedy for all our evils. I think he was greatly mistaken, as this bill means the con-

scription of the capital of the retired farmer and the ruination of the credit of the farming class.
Throughout the beautiful countryside of the province of Quebec you will find, Mr. Chairman, in nearly every village, fifteen or twenty retired farmers who, after having worked their farms during twenty, thirty or forty years and, in most cases, raised a large family, are ending their days in the shadow of the village church. Through the practice of economy, they have succeeded in setting aside for their old days from $4,000 to $10,000, and sometimes more. These worthy farmers, who have spent their lives on the land, have, in many cases, invested their all in first and second mortgages on farms. In our province, as you know, very little investment money comes to rural regions from outside; most of the mortgages are held by retired farmers in the villages and the surrounding country.
This infamous act, in force since last year, has given the worst possible results. It provides that if a farmer goes to the representative appointed by the government in each county to effect compromises between creditors and debtors and hands him the list of his debts, the receiver will immediately call upon the creditors to appear before him and, in many cases, the amount due by the farmer is reduced from forty to fifty per cent. Can it be considered reasonable to take away nearly half the savings of a worthy farmer who has toiled during forty or fifty years to provide himself with a small nest egg? I repeat, Mr. Chairman, that it is a crying injustice. A prime minister who proposes the adoption of such a law proves by the very fact that he knows nothing of the distress of the farming population of the province of Quebec.
Our farmers are quite willing to pay their debts, but, in order that they may do so, we must assist them instead of acting as the government does. Since this government came to power, they have done everything possible to penalize the farmer. First, they have not kept their pledges of 1930. The Prime Minister had promised everyone better prices for their products; he was to open new markets abroad, and thus relieve the situation. But, on the contrary, since he came to power, year after year he levied new taxes on farmers and, by this great bill, he takes away from them what was their most valuable assest, and that is credit. In the rural centres, nobody will now lend money to farmers because of bill No. 10. Why has the government such a grudge against the farming community, seeing that they ruin their credit; and why have

Farmers' Creditors Act- Mr. Gagnon
they such a gnulge against the small investor, the rentier, seeing that they are conscripting the capital which it took so many years for that man to gather? Why is the government always going after the small investor instead of the big capitalist?
The right hon. the Prime Minister, who, on more than one occasion, has paraded as a dictator after the fashion of Mussolini and Hitler, ought to read in the papers how Hitler is acting to get the money he needs, He does not go after the poor fellow only; he begins with those who have wealth. Our Prime Minister would do well to follow that example; he would do well to assist those who have no money and to get the money from those who possess it.

by the hon. member for Bonaventure (Mr. Marcil) is well taken. It is true that in the province of Quebec there is a moratorium whereby a creditor who has a claim guaranteed by a mortgage on a farm cannot sue the debtor if that debtor has paid his interest and his taxes. Of course that legislation is only of a temporary character, and if I were too much of a partisan I might take the view, a view which has been taken in some quarters, that the moratorium may have helped to destroy the credit of the farmers. I will not make that statement, however, because I want to approach the problem from a non-partisan standpoint. We must realize, however, that the moratorium legislation is only of a temporary character.
This new legislation, however, will have the effect of settling once and for all the difficulty existing between farmers and their creditors. When a farmer and his creditor appear before an official receiver they have the opportunity to agree upon a settlement which will give a satisfactory arrangement to both. According to information apparently in the possession of many hon. members it would appear that in many cases in the province of Quebec the amount of the claim registered against the farm has not been changed, and that only the rate of interest has been affected. In some cases money has been loaned at rates of five per cent, six per cent or seven per cent, and now we hear that creditors and debtors have gone before a board of review and in some instances have agreed to reduce the rate to two per cent or three per cent. I believe we cannot too greatly congratulate creditors who have such a commendable sense of justice as to reduce

interest rates to such an extent. A creditor who would do that ought to receive the congratulations of every hon. member because he shows he is endowed with humanitarian principles. In some cases the amount of the claim has not been changed, but the creditor and farmer have agreed to postpone the date of settlement.
All these details go to show that this legislation will not deprive the creditor of his legitimate rights, but will serve to indicate that it is a law of compromise and one which will tend to make for peace between the debtor and creditor. Once a debtor has made an amicable and equitable settlement with his creditor his credit is restored. It may be advisable to pass an amendment to the law whereby it would be enacted that the legislation we are now passing would not affect future deeds. I realize that in the future some people may have difficulty getting money from rentiers. An amendment might be suggested whereby it would be enacted that in the future this legislation would affect only past transactions. However, I leave that matter to the judgment of the house and for the attention of the Minister of Finance.
There is another aspect of the legislation which I desire to bring to the attention of the minister. If hon. members will read sections 2, 3, 4, 5 and 6 of chapter 53 of the statutes for 1934, namely:	The Farmers'
Creditors Arrangement Act, they would find that that legislation is complementary to the Bankruptcy Act, because the official receivers are given powers which belong to receivers under the Bankruptcy Act. I would respectfully draw the attention of the minister to the fact that in 1932 we amended the Bankruptcy Act and the effect of that amendment was that the Bankruptcy Act does not now apply to the farmers of the province of Quebec. In other words, whilst the farmers of other provinces may go into bankruptcy and make an arrangement with their creditors under the Bankruptcy Act, the farmers in the province of Quebec have no such rights, and that might be dangerous because of section 6 of the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act, 1934, which reads as follows:
(1)	A farmer who is unable to meet his liabilities as they become due may make a proposal for a composition, extension of time or scheme or arrangement either before or after an assignment has been made.
(2)	Such proposal shall be filed with the official receiver who shall forthwith convene a meeting of the creditors and perform the duties and functions required by the Bankruptcy Act

Farmers' Creditors Act-Mr. Gobeil
to be performed by a trustee in the case of a proposal for a composition, extension of time or scheme of arrangement.
Now if the official receiver gives a notice of discontinuance of proceedings, for instance, his rights might be impeached because a creditor might argue before the courts of the province of Quebec that the powers which the receiver has are very limited in nature because he gets his powers from under the Bankruptcy Act, and the Bankruptcy Act does not apply to the province of Quebec. I wonder if it would not be worth while to refer that point to the Department of Justice to find out whether it would be necessary to amend the Bankruptcy Act. But I may be too presumptuous; the minister may have an answer. Nevertheless we read in the newspapers of the city of Quebec that a creditor is serving notice upon the attorney general and the Minister of Justice that this bill which we are discussing is unconstitutional. I do not see myself why it would be ultra vires; I cannot see why the creditor would allege its so-called unconstitutionality. Since the matter is pending before the courts it might be wiser not to discuss it further, but in view of the litigation which is going on perhaps it would be wise to study the question anew from all angles so as to prevent any abuse of the rights of creditors before the courts.
May I finish my humble remarks with the wish that the negotiations which are now pending before the hon. Minister of Finance and the attorney general of Quebec may be successful. I do hope that a way will be found whereby the rights of a creditor whose rights are guaranteed by a deed of sale under a clause of redemption might be recognized. On the other hand, the debtor will be able to redeem his property and make an equitable settlement with his creditors and hope for better times.

I have just a few vrords to say about this legislation. I shall not follow the hon. member for Dorchester (Mr. Gagnon) in regard to the provincial field. I have not the advantage of being under the illusion of being a chief of a great party because I never went to the Sherbrooke convention. But I will discuss this matter simply as we have it before us. The hon. gentleman says that he is doubtful about this act having the force of law in Quebec because in 1932 there had been an amendment to the Bankruptcy Act, excluding farmers from its provisions. I would direct his attention to this Compromise and Arrangement between Farmers and Creditors Act, article 2, subsection 2, which reads:
This act shall be read and construed as one with the Bankruptcy Act, but shall have full force and effect notwithstanding anything contained in the Bankruptcy Act, and the provisions of the Bankruptcy Act and bankruptcy rules shall, except as in this act otherwise provided, apply mutatis mutandis in the case of proceedings hereunder including meetings of creditors.
I do not know if I am giving a wrong, interpretation of this section, but in my opinion it means that this legislation will apply to the whole country notwithstanding anything contained in the Bankruptcy Act. Hon. members on the other side have discussed special cases, as examples to show that this legislation is of advantage to both farmers and creditors. I do not think we should discuss this question on that basis. We should consider whether the present legislation and the proposed amendment are so drafted as to give power to the board of review and the officers to force a creditor to
[Mr. Porteous.l
reduce his claim even if it is secured as provided in section 7 of the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act, which reads:
A proposal may provide for a compromise or an extension of time or a scheme of arrangement in relation to a debt owing to a secured creditor, or in relation to a debt owing to a person who has acquired movable or immovable property subject to a right of redemption, but in that event the concurrence of the secured creditor or such person, shall be required, except in the case of a proposal formulated and confirmed by the board of review as hereinafter provided.
My interpretation of this section is that even if the creditor refuses the proposal of the debtor-farmer the case may go to the board of review, which in the province of Quebec is composed of a judge of the superior court, a representative of the creditor and a representative of the farmer. If that board of review decides from any consideration whatever that the creditor, whether secured or not, shall reduce his claim, its judgment is final, there is no appeal. That is the law as it stands to-day, and this section 7 is not to be amended by the present bill. That legislation is I submit unconstitutional, because it infringes on the provincial jurisdiction over property and civil rights. If it has not been applied in the province of Quebec, as stated by an hon. member on the other side, I am under the impression it is because the judges are reluctant to apply it anticipating that such judgment would be appealed and reversed. Nevertheless the law is there, and I submit that as it stands now the board of review can reduce the claim of a secured creditor; as we say in our civil code he may reduce hypothecatory claims just as well as ordinary claims. Consequently I believe that is unconstitutional.
If you permit me I shall discuss this legislation from another angle. We have the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act. A few days ago we passed the second reading of the Canadian Farm Loan Act. By that act a farmer will be allowed under certain conditions to borrow money from this country. Let me take a definite case: suppose a farmer from the county of my friend the hon. member for Dorchester makes application to borrow money from this government to cover indebtedness already incurred due to the crisis or to lack of a market or any other cause. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not believe I spoke last year when the original bill was under consideration, but I should like to say a few words on the second reading of this amending bill. The measure passed last year, together with the present bill, did not arise out of any local difficulty affecting the farming community of western Canada or that of eastern Canada; they arose out of conditions which really constitute a national problem. It is a mistake for us to consider that this is a question concerning farmers only. So far as we in the west are concerned I think we recognize the fact that it is absolutely essential for the well being and advancement of the west that agriculture should be assisted and developed to the greatest extent possible. One of the most pressing problems in Canada to-day is that arising out of the terrible burden placed on the people of the country through the financial position of our railways, particularly of the Canadian National Railways. I think we are all agreed that the only possible solution of our railway problem is to increase our population. Certainly it would be disastrous to have the population of the agricultural sections of the west depleted, and if there were no other reason than our railway problem it

seems to me that the need for helping, supporting and developing agriculture in the west would be one of major importance.
In passing, Mr. Speaker, let me say that I do not think the population of the west can be increased in any way other than through the development of agriculture. I cannot conceive of the development of industry in the west to any great extent unless it is developed by reason of the growth of the agricultural community which may furnish a home market for local industry. Apart from that there is another aspect of the matter which to, me is extremely important, namely that unless the burden pressing down so many of the farmers in the west is mitigated or relieved, and unless farmers who are on the verge of deciding to give up farming because it has ceased to pay are encouraged to remain on their farms, the result will be that in western Canada we shall have large numbers of derelict farms. That of itself would be a calamity. I know that there are parts of western Canada in which the farms have been vacated and have become the seed beds for weeds, with the result that weeds have spread to surrounding lands. Every derelict farm is a menace to all the farms in the immediate neighbourhood. The mortagees or the municipal officials who have taken possession of such farms, due to default in payments of mortgage indebtedness or of taxes are immediately burdened with the additional expense of keeping down the weeds. If they do not keep them down, the provincial weed inspector comes down on them, and they find themselves in difficulties. I cannot conceive of any greater calamity to western Canada or any greater blow to agriculture than that which would result in any considerable abandonment of farms. I view this not as a problem affecting only the farmer and not as a matter concerning only the industry of agriculture, but as a national problem which must be solved if the west is to be developed. If the west is not developed the railway problem becomes aggravated, and the financial burden involved in that great problem magnified to a considerable extent. For these reasons I support the second reading of the bill.

Mr. Speaker, when the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act was passed last year there was not a dissenting voice. In

Farmers' Creditors Act-Mr. Rhodes
this chamber the principle was adopted unanimously, and so far as I am aware no objection was taken to the passing of the bill. The principle of the bill having thus been accepted, and in view of the fact that the present measure does not disturb that principle but is designed merely for the purpose of eliminating one or * two minor defects which have been discovered in the operation of the act, and to improve the machinery for its operation, and inasmuch as there was no question of the principle of the bill being disturbed, I offered no observations in moving the second reading. That I was right in my assumption is with two exceptions evidenced by the remarks of different hon. members who have spoken. It has remained for the hon. member for Megantic (Mr. Roberge) to exhibit absolute hostility to the bill, and for the hon. member for Laprairie-Napierville (Mr. Dupuis) to call in question its constitutionality and in other respects perhaps to indicate that he is not altogether in agreement with its principle.
The hon. member for Megantic may represent the opinion of the farmers in his constituency who, he states, number 5,000. May I observe however that in recent months I have received not dozens but hundreds of letters not only from farmers but from other individuals. Many other people whom in the very nature of things I would not see at all have come to the department, and I have as yet to receive the first letter from a farmer or an individual complaining about the principle of the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act. To me that seems a remarkable circumstance, if in fact the hon. member for Megantic is speaking for the citizens in his constituency.
I could not help contrasting his remarks with those of the hon. member for Rosetown (Mr. Loucks) who agreed with the principle of the bill but thought it did not go far enough. On the other hand the hon. member for Megantic was bitterly opposed to the principle and said it went altogether too far. The hon. member for Laprairie-Napierville left the impression that the effect of this bill was to humiliate the farmer. As was quite properly pointed out by the hon. member for West Edmonton (Mr. Stewart) no farmer need be humiliated. He need not call into operation the provisions of the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act. I do not believe any farmer who does take advantage of the act need feel humiliated. What would be the object of his availing himself of its provisions? He would do so to place himself in a position to meet his obligations according to his ability. If a farmer is able to meet his obligations without referring to the act there is no necessity for his doing so.
I have not taken extensive notes, for the obvious reason that the queries which have been put to me are those which could best be answered when we are in committee of the whole, when a better opportunity for questions and answers is afforded. At that time I shall be pleased to give information in detail and to answer the questions of the hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Luch-kovich). Apparently the hon. member for Laprairie-Napierville is confused between the meanings of the word "social" and "socialism." This is social legislation, but it is as far removed from even the pink type of socialism as are the poles. What is the object of the legislation? The object is to keep the farmer on the farm, and surely if there is a capitalist on earth it is the farmer.
What I have said with respect to the questions of the hon. member for Vegreville applies also to references made by the hon. member for Dorchester (Mr. Gagnon). It is true that I have had some correspondence with Hon. L. A. Tasehereau, Premier of Quebec, and I should be very glad to produce it. I appreciate the difficulties in dealing with an old established law and, as may be necessary, in interfering with the civil code. While as yet there has been no legislation passed in the province of Quebec, my letter received a most cordial response from, the premier, and I feel sure if he can arrange an amendment to the law which will make for a more harmonious operation of this act, he will do so. We must remember that to the extent that the law of the province of Quebec militates against the successful operation of on one hand the farm loan act and on the other the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act, just to that extent it militates against the citizens of that province. I have every reason to believe that the government representative of the people of the province of Quebec will take such steps as may be open to it to make the privileges possible under this act available to the citizens of that province, in the same manner as they have been made available to the citizens in other provinces. It must be borne in mind that this act has been in operation only a few short months, and yet notwithstanding that circumstance there have to our knowledge been many hundreds of settlements made outside the scope of the act altogether, but arrived at in virtue of the fact that the parties knew that if resort was had to the act a setlement would be effected. In addition to that, we actually have to-day proposals before the official receivers in the various parts of Canada exceeding seven thousand in number. When it is borne in

Yes, there are peat bogs
in Ontario, and I presume in many countries of the world. In conjunction with the provinces Canada did at one time make an effort to investigate the possibility of converting these peat bogs into sources of useful fuels. A long series of investigations ensued under what I believe was known as the peat fuel committee. As a result a plant was set up at Alfred, a point between here and Montreal, and an expenditure of about $350,000 was made. The experiments did not prove successful. Other efforts were made in Saskatchewan with regard to lignite, and large sums of money were spent.
Was that not a briquetting experiment?

They got

fuel comparable with the domestic fuel used in the central provinces. I have heard considerable talk about it, particularly in the last two or three weeks. It may be that a process has been developed which will provide an additional source of domestic fuel.

I propose to study the matter further because if the process is perfected to the point where it will produce from these peat bogs what the proponents of the process say it will produce, then it is something which any government, provincial or federal, should investigate so that such a fuel could be placed on the market. In the meantime I purpose continuing my investigations of the possibilities of this new process which the sponsors say will develop fuel from peat bogs. I have an open mind on the subject; I do not know whether the process is good, bad or indifferent, but I shall continue my investigations and find out the amount of success there was in Denmark, where I believe a plant has been recently set up, and the success in Ireland where similar operations are being projected.

coal. speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext:
Each year a plan of geological survey work is .mapped out by the departmental officials, and it is largely determined by the assignment of a part of the vote to carry on geological work that has been already started and is under way where it is sought to have a regular progression of the work take place, and by turning towards those areas where information would seem to indicate that geological work would determine favourable occurrences for the deposition of minerals which like gold can easily be disposed of. Those are the factors that underlie the mapping out of the year's geological work. The plan of the work for this year is now under consideration. Perhaps I could not do better than to read a short memorandum that has been prepared in the department, after consultation with myself on a great many occasions, as to the general plan for this year:
Geological and topographical work to aid prospecting for and development of gold placers and other mineral deposits in the Yukon.
Geological and topographical work in the Bridge river area of British Columbia, an active gold producing camp.
The investigation of gold' bearing deposits on Vancouver island.
Geological exploration of regions bordering the lower Fraser river on the west.
That area, as the members from British Columbia know, is almost an unknown area in the province, but an area in which mineral deposits have beeen discovered.
Supply-Geological Survey

Investigation of gold bearing deposits in the Barkerville and adjacent areas in British Columbia.
Investigation of various gold bearing and other mineral discoveries in southern British Columbia.
That, broadly speaking, is the plan that is now under consideration by the branch of the geological service with respect to the work for this year in British Columbia. Their work will be devoted, as I have indicated, to those sections where it is known that the progress of the work is likely to disclose that kind of geological occurrence that is most favourable for the deposition of ores that are more easily sold than others, gold in particular.
After the explorers have been in the districts mentioned and made their discoveries, is the information they have gathered disseminated to the public, or is it kept within the department itself?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext: Just as soon as the year's work is mapped out and determined, the program is made known by the department through the technical publications. Then when the field parties return to Ottawa from their year's geological work, their field notes and other information with respect to the areas in which they have operated are with all reasonable dispatch converted into a formal report which is printed as one of the publications of the department and made available as soon as possible to those interested, prospectors, the mineral industry, and to anyone who cares to inquire.

I think the work done by this branch is money well spent and that the work is well carried out under a competent head. Would the minister give us more details of the work that is proposed to be done on Vancouver island, and where it is to be done?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext:
I cannot say whether the
department has received any direct specific request for investigations in the first named field, but negotiations are at present going on between the officers of the government of British Columbia and our own department, with a view to having geological work carried on where, in the best judgment of those who are perhaps most familiar with the locality, it will be of greatest use. I am in thorough accord with what has been said by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni, and I am sure it commends itself to all other hon. members, that no more useful work can be carried on in what is generally called the northern part of Canada than geological research work, particularly for precious metals. That work has been going on, as hon. members know, since 1842, as a department of some government, though not then of course the dominion government. But the first director of geological survey was Sir William Logan, and the work has been carried on continuously down to the present time. Personally I should like to see it greatly extended. Of course, none of us will ever see the time when even fairly well known mining areas will have been completely explored geologically. I well remember that at a meeting of the institute of mining and metallurgy not many years ago a person who should have known better suggested that, this work having been carried on in Canada since 1842, it was strange that they did not know all about the geological occurrences of the country by now. Well, if anyone will review the history of Britain he will find that for hundreds of years geological records have been kept of the work done there, a very small country compared with Canada; and last year they had a larger vote than ever devoted to geological work in Britain. At least therefore we can get some comfort from the reflection that there will be activities in geological work in Canada for hundreds of years to come, and then we shall know very little about the riches that may be hidden, not sticking out for people to go and dig them up easily, but hidden where they will challenge the curiosity and the courage of the people of to-day and of those who will come after us.

Supply-Geological Survey

Are any
other departments of government carrying on geological survey work, or is this the only geological survey provided?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext:
This is the only one that
the dominion government is carrying on. Some provincial governments in later years have started geological work, principally in Ontario and latterly in Quebec. I doubt whether there is any in the other provinces. Where Ontario and Quebec carry on geological survey work, it was the practice of the late government, a very proper practice too, as it is of the present government, to have a meeting perhaps once or twice a year to see that the provincial work did not overlap the work that was being done by the dominion. That is essential, because it is only throwing money away to have a second set of geologists going over the same field that is being pursued by this government.

I am glad that there is an increase in this vote, and I am pleased to have heard the minister's explanation, because in my opinion any assistance given to the exploration of our natural resources must be taken seriously. I notice that the daipartment is working in conjunction with the mines department of British Columbia. The Department of Mines in that province, especially in the northern portion, is making investigations and sending suggestions to this department, and I am glad to know that recommendations are coming from the province for further explorations. I am sure from what the minister has said that the matter will be given the consideration it deserves.
Has any survey investigation been made in Quebec and, if so, how much was expended out of the $190,000 last year?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext: Yes; there is geological survey work being done in the province of Quebec, but I have not before me the amount actually expended. However, from the chart I have before me, I should say that there was more money spent in geological survey work in the province of Quebec last year than in any other province. That of course, as the hon. member knows, arises from the fact-
The discovery of a new field.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext:
Yes, the very valuable discoveries that were made at Noranda and to the northeast through Chibougamau. There
is also keen interest being taken in the development not only of gold mining but copper mining and the mining of other metals in the northern part of the province. This may give my hon. friend some information. I see that more parties were sent into Quebec last year than into any other province. Quebec is now doing some geological work itself. Ontario of course has for many years been expanding its geological work, and in order that overlapping may not take place the amount of work that the dominion government has been doing in Ontario is gradually becoming less. At the moment more work is being done in Quebec than elsewhere, although they are now developing a geological survey branch of their own, which I think is a verj desirable effort.
How much of this appropriation is devoted to the purposes of the geographic board of Canada? Is it all of the $75,502 or only part of it?

the board is made up of a number of officials drawn from various departments of government. The mines department supplies to the board the secretary whose salary is $2,160 a year. Just before this item carries and we conclude the estimates of the mines department, I would like to ask the minister to revert for a moment to Mr. Brown. I understand now that the government is going to undertake rather extensive experimental work at the instigation of Mr. Brown.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext: No, not at all.

Well, just what is this new experimental work that is being undertaken that he speaks of so highly as having originated in Denmark and having in some degree been carried on in Ireland in connection with peat fuel?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext:
I have before me no plan by Mr. Brown. He has seen me and talked to me about the promotion of a company for the manufacture and sale of peat fuel. He has told me that there is in Denmark a plant now operating. He has also told me that the great firm of Babcock and Wilcox, well known throughout the world, have approved the mechanical operations of a plant that was built to take advantage, I believe, of certain patent processes which the companies or individuals that he says he represents, hold with respect to the development of peat fuel. But let me not be misunderstood. There is at the present time so far as I am concerned no intention whatever with the information before me to advise the government to embark upon anything in the way of a project that Mr. Brown has of actually manufacturing peat or, as he suggests, to grant dominion government subsidies in connection with peat fuel until it is made abundantly apparent to me that the plant now in operation in Denmark or Ireland, or wherever it may be, is being conducted and operated on a sound business basis, producing a fuel which is a comparable, competitive fuel in the areas where it might be marketed in Ontario and Quebec. Even then a great deal of investigation work would have to be undertaken by somebody -and I think that somebody certainly comprises those who are advocating the adventure into peat fuel-before any government, whether provincial or dominion, would be justified in subsidizing peat fuel.

Let the committee remember, as I said before, that I have an absolutely open mind in the matter. If there is any fuel that can be provided at lower cost to the people in what we call the acute fuel area, that is the central portion of Canada, and that will better the situation to the consumer of fuel, then we or any other government would be derelict in our duty if we did not at least see that no barrier was thrown in the way of the development of that fuel. But it is quite a different matter as to the desirability of a government subsidizing a private activity of this character, and if the government could be persuaded to do this, it would in my judgment be only after the closest scrutiny as to the soundness not only of the process but of the economics that are involved in the distribution of the fuel. I do not think I can say more than that, but I would be extremely careful to see that when any steps were being taken, the closest scrutiny would be made of any plan that is projected for peat fuel. At the same time I have an open mind. There will undoubtedly come a time -it may be long delayed; it may not he so far away-when peat fuel may have to be resorted to, but at the same time I can only repeat what I said before; there would have to be a very complete disclosure of the soundness of a plan before I could be induced to recommend it to this or any other government for subsidy, because if these peat fuels are able to perform as some of their advocates say, they do not need any government assistance. However, I have the matter under consideration in the hope that more information will be available in order that I may make up my mind whether or not from a national standpoint it is of sufficient value to warrant further investigation.

Have any investigations been made into the possibilities of extracting oil and gasoline from coal? The minister no doubt knows that Great Britain was one of the greatest coal producing countries of the world until she lost the market when oil was introduced. Now many of her own battleships are using fuel oil. But Great Britain has seen the seriousness of the situation in the coal mining industry and I understand is making extensive experiments and has now discovered how to extract fuel oil and gasoline from coal. In vew of the fact that we have in Canada large coal fields, and are feeling the competition of fuel oil from abroad, I was wondering if the department had made any investigation into that matter.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext:
It is pretty well known that Germany and Great Britain for a number of years have spent through state agencies

Supply-Geological Survey
and private activity huge sums in endeavouring to develop some process to extract fuel oil and gasoline from coal on a commercial basis. Some advance has been made. Great Britain has done a great deal, and some fuel oil and gasoline have been produced commercially, but under a very heavy protective tariff, I think they call it. In Germany the protection is twenty-two cents a gallon, and in England apparently 8 pence. Some work has been done in investigation of the possibilites of extraction of oil and gasoline from our fuels. The advances made in research work by Great Britain are I believe available to us. I do not believe it would be a justifiable expense at present for Canada to set up a large and costly research staff to carry on this work when Great Britain is doing it. It is true that such investigation is also being carried on by private concerns in Great Britain and their results might not be as readily available to us as those from the work being done by the state. But I seriously question the wisdom of our doing more than we are at the moment, which I confess is not very much.

Referring again to the question of further experimental work on peat fuel, I think the minister is well advised to be cautious in touching any project that may be brought to him by a person whom he does not know and as to whose nationality even he seems to be in doubt, though his name is Brown. He will doubtless take into consideration also the fact that the situation in Denmark and Ireland is not the same as in this country. In one of them peat has been the traditional fuel used eVer since the country was an inhabited part of the globe; the peat there of course is entirely different from that in this country where it has a high liquid content. In Denmark the population is extremely dense, and in both those countries there are no wooded areas from which to draw fuel supplies, which are carefully preserved for other purposes than fuel. But in this country we still have abundant fuel resources, both underground in the form of coal and on the surface in the form of trees. Therefore I do not think there is any necessity at this time for further experimental work in connection with peat fuel, and I am glad the minister is giving the matter careful consideration before he goes into it again.

In reference to the remark made by the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Reid). I did not intend to deal with that matter-it seemed so hopeless -but as he has brought it up I join with him in pressing on the department the need for consideration being given to the subject
of making our large coal resources available in some form other than in the raw state. Their location makes it often difficult to market the product just as coal. I notice, and I am sorry to notice, the remark of the minister that they are not doing very much. I entirely agree with that; I do not think the Department of Mines are paying anything like the attention they ought to that branch of a very important subject. I will go further and say that I think the officials are wholly unsympathetic.

Well, that is my opinion, as a result of ten years', experience.

But I do not know, and I certainly shall not get my information from the department, 'because when I write them they say; "We have no information beyond newspaper accounts." I am not an official paid to give these subjects intensive study, but I get the information as soon as they do. I do think the. department should make a special effort to develop investigations, not along the line of elemental scientific discoveries but by taking advantage of the acquired knowledge of other peoples. In Great Britain, certainly where governmental aid is introduced, we could get that information readily enough; unless it is in connection with a distinctly private patent-which I do not think is the case here-I believe the British people are not unwilling to afford assistance to one of the dominions in this way.
I am not finding fault with the minister. I know the multitudinous duties he has to perform, and I know he has to rely on his various deputies. I do claim, however, that the officials of the mines department are not paying enough attention to this subject. One of the crying needs of Canada to-day is to get our coal mines working to capacity; we so much need work for coal miners. People are coming here every day asking the government to increase the subventions in order that coal may be shipped from one place in the country, where providence or nature has placed it, to the centres of population. It may be difficult bo transport coal as such, but it is easy to transport it in the shape of gasoline, fuel oil or the like. I am not saying this with any suggestion of political antagonism to the minister; rather I am asking that he use his influence to stir up that branch of his department and get some action.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext: The department would have to be greatly enlarged to undertake work like that.

I just wish to direct the attention of the hon. member for Bow River to the fact that there need be no doubt in the world as to the nationality of Mr. Brown. He is a native of Prince Edward Island, and therefore he is a citizen of no mean country.

Mr. STEWART (Edmonton); What proportion of this amount is used for the movement of coal from Alberta eastward?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext:
Perhaps I can give both east and west at the same time; it might shorten the discussion. The total of eastern coal moved under subvention in 1984 was 1,824,656 tons, at a cost of $1,729,552.81. The total of western coal moved under subvention was 544,147 tons at a total cost of $531,610.86. The total moved was 2,368,803 tons at a total cost of $2,261,163.67.
Mr. REID; I wonder if the minister can tell us if any of that money went to _ coal moving from Alberta to British Columbia or vice versa?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext: No, none of this money was devoted to coal moving from Alberta to British Columbia.
Do those figures include the movement of coal from the Estevan coal fields in Saskatchewan?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext: Yes.

Has there been any change in the subvention rate in connection with the Estevan coal? A year or two ago the rate from the Saskatchewan coal fields was very much reduced, and I wondered if there had been any change in that rate during the last year or so.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext:
In May of last year the coal operators of Saskatchewan, Alberta and British Columbia came to Ottawa with the idea of trying to adjust the coal subventions in order as nearly as possible to bring the assistance into a horizontal shape, if I may put it in that way, so that one would not

be preferred over another. At that time there was a general scaling down of the subventions, it being found that mainly by reason of subventions which had been granted for quite a number of years, and which were increased in the last three and a half years, the Manitoba market is largely and almost entirely supplied by the coal mines of Alberta, the Crowsnest and Saskatchewan. I may say that the meeting of the coal operators was not acrimonious at all. They recognized that the subventions they had been getting had secured practically the entire Manitoba market, and that the rates then effective were no longer necessary. Therefore there was a gradation downward of the subventions with respect to the coal of all three provinces coming into Manitoba, and it applied with equal force, as nearly as we could determine it, to each of the coal fields. So far as I know there has been no great complaint made by the operators since. I am very glad to tell the house that with the least possible expense to the state the coal mines both east and west have been able to reach further into the great consuming part of Canada. I need not tell hon. members how extremely difficult this whole matter has been and will continue to be, because we cannot change our geographical situation or our political boundaries. Mistakes will be made. I know that my administration of this most complex question has not been without error, and I am happy in the thought that perhaps all my errors have not yet been found out. At any rate we are endeavouring as best we can to apply these subventions throughout Canada, both east and west, in order that the maximum amount of Canadian coal may be consumed in Canada and the greatest number of Canadian coal miners may get work.

The minister mentioned a meeting last year. I wondered if there was any change with regard to the basis on which this subvention is paid. Is it still on a mileage basis or is it just a flat rate of so much per ton?
While the minister is looking up that point I might say that when the subvention first * operated, I believe about 1930, the rate from the Estevan coal mine was 25 cents a ton to Winnipeg. I believe the rate from Alberta was set at about one dollar a ton. Then two or three years ago it was changed and put on a mileage basis of one-seventh of a cent per mile. The Estevan coal mines being about 280 miles from Winnipeg the subvention was reduced from 25 cents down to about 15 cents, or approximately that amount I wonder if any change has been made since.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext: The prevailing rate is one-seventh of a cent per ton mile from Saskatchewan with a maximum of 15 cents to Manitoba. That was the change made to which the hon. member has referred.
